paper_title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents now do much of their work through tools. They search literature databases, look up genes and proteins, query sample catalogs and book travel by calling APIs, and they build their answers from what those APIs return. The agents answer can only be as good as the tool results it reads. Most of the time, broken tool call is easy to see, because the API returns an error, times out or sends malformed data. Some failures leave no such trace. Consider an agent that asks catalog API how many samples match two conditions. The APIs documentation names one filter slightly wrong, so the API ignores that filter and counts the samples that match the other condition alone. The response 1 is well formed, the status is 200, and the number is wrong. We call such response silent API failure. It looks successful but does not answer the request that was sent. We call its cause silent fault. Neither is rare. Among 15 public research APIs, 11 answer at least one plausible mistake this way, by ignoring misnamed filter, dropping filter value with typo or quietly cutting page short (5.1). Earlier work shows that agents miss silent tool errors (Sun et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026) and that production APIs fail silently when constraint is stated only in prose (Li et al., 2026). In our faults the response is well formed and consistent with itself, so no check on the response alone can show the fault. It takes extra queries to the same API. The fixes in use today put the model in charge. checklist prompt asks it to inspect each result (Sun et al., 2024). reviewer model checks each call (Ta et al., 2026). Outcome Monitors attach warning to suspect results (Panthi and Abdelfattah, 2026), and an LLM judge rates them. In our tests, each of these leaves wrong answers close to the 74.0% of an unguarded agent. The surprising part is why. The problem does not go unseen. judge that is shown the results of consistency check flags 82.4% of faulted runs (and 13.9% of clean runs), and plain warning from the check tells the agent that the result failed. The agent then reports the flagged count anyway, in 77.4% of the runs the judge flagged and in 64.4% of the runs that got warning. Agents are not blind to the flag, since their stated confidence drops and many mention the warning. They answer anyway. Controlled comparisons on 7 open models separate three ingredients  (Table 2)  . The first is evidence, test whose result shows that the response cannot be right. Without it, judge leaves about 70% of answers wrong, whether its verdict is advice (71.7%) or is enforced by blocking (70.8%). The second is permission. Agents default to giving number, and short prompt that allows the answer cannot be determined cuts wrong answers after warning from 70.1% to 18.2%. The cut is uneven (059% wrong by model), and the same prompt without evidence does nothing. The third is enforcement. When the harness (the code that runs the agents tool calls) decides what happens to failed result, the outcome depends far less on the model. harness that withholds the value leaves 1.7% wrong, at most 4% on any model. SilentGuard (Figure 1) applies these findings as invariant-aware harness enforcement. It produces evidence with invariants, properties that must hold on correct API. For filtered count, the count with condition plus the count with its negation must equal the count without it. For list, every returned record must meet the filter. Every request must use parameters the API documents. Where no exact invariant exists it uses contracts learned from clean responses. result that fails is re-checked once. What the harness does next depends on how certain the failed check is. broken exact invariant proves that the API did not answer the request, so the harness withholds the value and accepts only checked answers. learned check can itself be wrong, so the harness only warns. No extra model call is needed. Across 7 open models SilentGuard cuts wrong answers from 74.0% to 1.7% with no loss on fault-free (clean) tasks, and on three frontier models from 70.2% to 0.5% (5.3). On nine real APIs, given documentation in which we changed one filter name, wrong answers fall from 89.8% to 21.3%. check against the APIs published parameters does as well alone (21.0%). SilentGuard prevents wrong answers by abstaining, not by recovering. Under faults it mostly says the count cannot be determined, and it cannot see fault that keeps its checks true. So we report risk against coverage (Figure 2). At 25% fault rate SilentGuard answers 67% of tasks with 3.3% of its answers wrong, while methods without evidence, or with advice alone, stay near the 24.6% risk of no guard. SilentGuard also has limits. Blind retry does better on faults that clear within one or two calls. The parameter check cannot see filter written inside query string. Contributions. (1) measurement of silent failures in 15 real APIs, covering three kinds of fault. (2) Controlled comparisons showing that evidence is necessary, that most agents do not act on it unless told they may abstain, and that only enforcement by the harness is reliable across models. (3) SilentAgent tool call API HTTP 200 + result 1. Check the result exact: count identity, lists, spec learned: contracts from clean data fail pass Release to the agent 2. Re-check: same call once fail pass 3. Fails again: exact check? yes ( ˆαj τ ) no: learned Withhold Warn checked answers only keep value, say what failed Harness (SilentGuard) Figure 1: SilentGuard in the harness. Every tool result is checked, and result that fails is re-checked once. If it fails again, the harness withholds it when the failed check is exact and warns when the check is learned and may itself be wrong (Eq. 2). The model never decides alone whether result can be trusted. Guard, set of invariant checks enforced by the harness, which withholds results that fail an exact check and only warns on results that fail learned check. (4) AgentOrchBench, our benchmark with exact answers, and an evaluation with predictions written down in advance. The evaluation covers four benchmarks, count and list answers, published methods and controls, 7 open models, and 3 frontier models added later. Code and tasks are at https: //github.com/Sajib-006/silentguard.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Tool failures and agent robustness. Recent benchmarks inject failures into tool responses. They find that observation handling is where agents break (Zheng et al., 2026), that implicit failures hurt more than explicit errors (Zhu et al., 2026), and that reliability drops under production-like stress (Gupta, 2026; Tian et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Agents also claim success they did not achieve (Advani, 2026), stronger models can trust tool outputs more (Wang and Vemuri, 2026), and agents adopt corrupted tool returns even when they question them (Yang et al., 2026). Production APIs often accept queries they do not understand and still return HTTP 200 (Li et al., 2026). We study what agents do with such results and how the harness can catch them. 2 Fixes for unreliable tools. Warning the model that tools may fail and giving it checklist helps on simple tool errors (Sun et al., 2024). second model can review each tool call before it runs (Ta et al., 2026). Outcome Monitors learn contracts from clean traces and attach non-binding warning to results that break them (Panthi and Abdelfattah, 2026). Skeptical prompting and re-querying give mixed gains (Zhang et al., 2026a), and runtime layers check or wrap tool use (Zhao et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026; Mansoor et al., 2026). Code outside the model can also decide. Guardrail frameworks (Rebedea et al., 2023), secure agent designs (Debenedetti et al., 2025) and rule-based enforcement (Wang et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025) control which actions an agent may take. ToolGate commits tool result only when hand-written postcondition holds (Liu et al., 2026), deterministic gates block writes that break policy (Reddy et al., 2026), and final verifier can withhold whole episode (Zhang et al., 2026b). These check actions, hand-written conditions or whole episodes. We check each read result with exact identities that the harness tests by sending extra queries to the same API, and we show in controlled tests why the decision must leave the model. Checks without ground truth. Our count check is metamorphic relation (Chen et al., 1998; Segura et al., 2016), two-way form of the query partition used to find bugs in database engines (Rigger and Su, 2020). Metamorphic relations have been used to test REST APIs offline (Segura et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2026), and fuzzers such as RESTler (Atlidakis et al., 2019) look for crashes, not wrong answers. We run the check online, per call. Learned contracts follow specification and invariant mining (Ernst et al., 2007; Panthi and Abdelfattah, 2026). How models use evidence. LLMs often fail to correct their own answers without outside feedback (Huang et al., 2024). When the context contradicts what they believe, they may follow it or ignore it (Xie et al., 2024). We study the reverse case, in which the outside feedback is right and most models do not act on it unless told they may abstain. Models guess rather than abstain, because training and scoring reward guess (Kalai et al., 2025; Kirichenko et al., 2025). Agents invent values mainly when tool failure is not signalled (Sethi et al., 2026). Our faults are never signalled, and prompt that allows abstaining does nothing without evidence. Saying cannot be determined is form of abstention (Wen et al., 2025) and of selective prediction (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Kamath et al., 2020). Here the harness, not the model, decides when to abstain.

sections.content: Silent API failures. tool call is request and response r. silent failure is response with success status whose content does not answer q. For example, filter is ignored, condition is misread, or total is capped. Nothing in marks it. Checks. SilentGuard uses two kinds of check, depending on what the tool allows (App. B). Exact checks hold on any API that applies its filters correctly, so failure shows that the request was not answered as sent. For count queries we test, after every filter query, the count identity (F ) + (F<k Ck) = (F<k), (1) where (F ) is the count the API returns for filter = C1 Ck and F<k drops the last condition. The harness issues the two extra queries itself. For every position of the condition list we repeat the test, so an ignored filter anywhere is caught. When the answer is list of records, the harness also checks that every returned record meets the filter, that no record repeats, and that the list size matches the reported total. When an API publishes its parameter list, request with parameter outside it is rejected before it runs (the parameter check, or spec check). Learned checks come from clean traces and cover field presence and type, echoed arguments, positive values, categorical values, linear relations between fields and date order, mined as in Panthi and Abdelfattah (2026). Table 1 lists the checks by kind of tool operation, including ones we did not test. Detection and action. SilentGuard separates finding problem from acting on it. Each check maps tool result to pass or fail and has an estimated false-alarm rate ˆαj = 1/(nj + 2), where nj is the number of clean examples it held on (rule of succession). Exact checks are invariants that hold on every correct API. Learned checks are mined from clean responses and can raise false alarms. Of 84 documented operations in 13 public APIs, 61 allow an exact check and all allow the spec check  (Table 14)  . with cutoff τ = 1%. New checks plug into π without changing it. SilentGuard. For every tool result the harness runs the checks. (1) result that passes is released unchanged. (2) result that fails is re-checked once. The harness sends the same call again and releases the new result only if it passes. (3) If the result fails again, the action depends on the failed check (Eq. 2). If failed check is exact (ˆαj τ ), the failed values are withheld and the agent is told which values could not be verified and which other tool could redo the step. On count answers this becomes an answer rule. The harness accepts only count that passed check, rejects any other count twice, and then answers that the count cannot be determined. If failed check is learned from few examples, the data stays visible with warning naming the failed property and the recovery tools, as in Panthi and Abdelfattah (2026). (4) Results that already carry an error pass through unchanged. result checklist (Sun et al., 2024) is added to the system prompt. SilentGuard never repairs value on its own. Recovery is always the agents own call with listed tool (5.4 shows why). AgentOrchBench (ours). We built AgentOrchBench to measure silent failures where the right answer is known exactly. The agent works from shell and calls eight local REST services with curl, and all services are reset before each task. Each task asks how many of the 400 catalog records match two or three conditions, and the answer is single number computed from the seed data, so grading is exact and needs no judge. The catalog returns only the count, so the agent cannot check filter by reading the records. Faults are injected inside the server. The reply is HTTP 200, and the fault repeats on every call, so asking again returns the same wrong number. Each fault type is modeled on kind of API bug (Table 7, App. A.1). One of them, an ignored parameter, is the failure we measure in real public APIs (5.1). We ran the six fault types in the top part of Table 7. The two below them keep the count identity true by design and are used in the list tasks and the harness-only tests (App. and I). retail orders API with four fault types tests whether results carry over to different schema. We ran 36 tasks with 2 seeds under each fault type and with no fault, for every model and method variant (arm). Other benchmarks. The real public APIs are 9 APIs (NCBI, UniProt, Europe PMC, GBIF, Zenodo, ChEMBL, arXiv, DataCite, iNaturalist) with 5 count tasks each and correct or slightly wrong documentation. That gives 45 runs per model, arm and documentation version. ToolMaze (Zhu et al., 2026) has 400 multi-step tool workflows with silent faults that hit the first call (P3) or every call (P4), explicit errors (P1, P2) and clean runs (P0), scored by its own judge (App. A.3). We used 180 workflows never used in method design. Methods compared. The published methods are checklist prompt (Sun et al., 2024), reviewer (Ta et al., 2026) and Outcome Monitors (OM) (Panthi and Abdelfattah, 2026). The reviewer is the agents own model, which checks each call before it runs for up to five loops. OM uses its contract miner and warning text, with rules learned from clean responses of other tasks. On ToolMaze we also run the checklist plus OM. The baselines and controls are no guard, caution prompt, an LLM judge in the sense of Zheng et al. (2023), self-verification, blind retry (every call sent twice, the second response released) and re-query (both 4 responses shown). The judge is fixed model (gptoss-120b) that also sees the check results, meaning the harnesss consistency queries. The ablations of the harness action are warning, warning with recovery tip, answer gate, Enforce (checked counts only, failed count left visible) and auto-repair (the harness recounts by another route). Prompts are in App. C. Models. The main runs use 7 open-weight (open) models (Phi-4, gpt-oss-120b, Gemma-327B, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-4-Scout, Llama-4Maverick and Nemotron-3-Ultra). Three frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna) ran six arms of AgentOrchBench and two arms of the realAPI study (5.3). The frontier AgentOrchBench runs and the Nemotron-3-Ultra control arms ran on Genentechs internal platform with the same code, tasks, seeds and grader. Company policy bars releasing their logs, so we report their answer counts. All models use at most 2,000 output tokens per turn, at most 16 turns (25 on ToolMaze) and the same prompts. The open models run at temperature 0, and the frontier models use the provider default (App. D). Protocol. Every planned experiment was written down with its predictions before it ran. The code was frozen by hash, and runs refuse to start if the code changed. The method went through three versions on ToolMaze. Each version was tested only on unseen workflows, and the final SilentGuard was frozen before all planned runs (App. F). Grading and statistics. We grade each answer as correct (it equals the ground truth), unknown (it gives no count) or wrong (any other count). Confidence values and identifiers are not read as counts. ToolMaze uses its own judge. We report the mean over models with its standard error (SE, ) and 95% task-cluster bootstrap intervals for the key differences. We also report how many of the 7 models show the difference, with an exact sign-flip test (smallest 0.016, App. D).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Silent API failures are common in real services and fool every agent we tested. The fixes in use today leave the decision to the model, which by default reports the number it was given, even when it is told the number is suspect. Evidence of the fault is necessary, and permission to abstain lets some models act on it. Only enforcement by the harness works for every model. Harness builders should give the harness the final say over results that fail an exact check, and repair only fault types the check can confirm. API builders should reject unknown parameters and say when page was cut. Benchmarks should include faults that repeat.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Checks have blind spots. fault that is consistent with itself (prefix matching) and an API that knows the check (the consistent lie) both pass count checks, and filter the agent never sends cannot be checked. SilentGuard leaves these wrong. What exact assumes. The count identity assumes two-valued filters. Fields with missing values need the three-way partition of Rigger and Su (2020), which we do not use, and totals that are estimated or change between queries can break the identity. The identity held on all 25 live queries we tried, which is small sample. The valueswap check compares live counts too. In the valueformat study, four wrong answers passed because the total changed slightly between the request and the check. An exact check can also fire when the reported value is right (the ignore-NOT fault breaks the checks own queries), and those runs are scored as faulted, not clean. Saying unknown. Under faults, SilentGuard mostly answers that the count cannot be determined. This is the safe answer when the API cannot give correct one, but it gives the user no number. Models. Seven open-weight models ran every agent experiment. Three frontier models from one vendor ran six arms of the main benchmark and two of the real-API study. These frontier runs and the control arms of Nemotron-3-Ultra ran on Genentechs internal platform, so we have their answer counts but cannot release or recount their logs, and we have no hash records for them. Those runs were added after the planned experiments, with no predictions. Seven models limit the power of model-level tests. Short faults and false alarms. Blind retry beats SilentGuard on faults that clear within one or two calls (5.3), and learned checks cost some clean success on ToolMaze. Method design. The method went through three versions, and each was tested on fresh data. The 1% cutoff τ was chosen after seeing earlier results, but any cutoff below 1.85% gives the same decisions. Benchmarks. Our fault injectors run on our own APIs. The real-API probes show that ignored filters, silently capped pages and ignored filter values occur in practice. The other fault types are not measured in real APIs. On further benchmark (τ -bench) SilentGuard tied the published methods (App. J).

sections.content: This section gives the tasks, faults and grading of each benchmark. 11 A.1 AgentOrchBench Agent protocol. The agent solves one task per run. In each turn it writes exactly one of RUN: <one curl command> or ANSWER: <answer>, and after each RUN it receives the HTTP status and the response body. Pipes, other shell commands and file access are not allowed. All eight local services (among them sample registry, metadata catalog and task tracker, on ports 8001 to 8008) are reset before every task, so runs do not affect each other. Tasks. The 36 count tasks each ask how many of the 400 catalog records match two (15 tasks) or three (21 tasks) conditions, for example How many catalog assets have QC_Status=qc-pass AND Sample_Type=tumor? Return: count=<n>. The ground truth is computed from the seed data. The records are synthetic, so no model can know count from its training data. Fault injection. Faults are switched on inside the catalog server for whole run. The server echoes the fault mode back, and the runner refuses to start if the echo does not match, so run can never use the wrong fault. Every fault returns HTTP 200 and well-formed body, and repeats on every call. The catalog returns only the count (total_count), as real aggregation endpoint does. With full records returned, model could check the filter by reading them. Table 7 lists the fault types and the kind of bug each is modeled on. otherwise. sections.title: B Implementation of SilentGuard
sections.content: This section gives the checks, the cutoff rule and the exact messages the agent sees. Count check. For filter query = C1 Ck that returns , the harness checks each position i. It queries the other conditions without Ci (count Ti) and with Ci (count Mi), and tests + Mi = Ti. That is 2k extra queries per filter call (at most 6 here). On any API that applies AND and NOT correctly the identity holds, so the check cannot fire on correct count. fault that keeps the identity true (prefix matching, consistent lie) passes it. fault that breaks the negation queries themselves (ignore NOT) makes the check fire although the reported count may be right. Spec check and value-swap check. When an API publishes its parameter list, request with parameter outside the list is stopped before it runs, and the agent gets an error instead of silently wrong result. For parameter that is in the list, the harness re-issues the query with the filters value swapped. If the count does not change, the filter was ignored. Learned checks. On ToolMaze we used the Outcome Monitors contract miner (Panthi and Abdelfattah, 2026), which covers presence and type, echoed arguments, positive values, categorical values, linear relations and date order. Contracts are mined from clean responses of other workflows with 5-fold cross-fitting by task, so contract is never mined on the workflow it checks. Cutoff. check that held on clean examples gets the false-alarm estimate 1/(n + 2) (rule of succession). Exact identities and the spec check count as = . If any failed check has an estimate of at most the cutoff τ = 1%, the failed values are withheld. Otherwise the result stays visible with warning. With the few clean examples ToolMaze provides, no learned contract reaches the cutoff, so on ToolMaze SilentGuard always warns. Messages shown to the agent. After count fails the check twice, the agent sees the response with the count removed and the following note. total_count withheld: this result failed an exact consistency check twice (the harness already reran the request). Do not guess the count; re-query differently, or answer that the count cannot be determined. If the agent then answers with count that did not pass the check, the harness replies (at most twice, after which it answers that the count cannot be determined) as follows. HARNESS: answer rejected. The count you report is not the count of query that passed the consistency check. Re-query in way that yields verified count, or answer that the count cannot be determined. count is treated as verified only if it came from query that passed the check and that has at least as many conditions as any other query in the run. This stops check passed on looser query from backing count for the full filter. Result checklist. SilentGuard adds this checklist, written in the style of Sun et al. (2024), to the system prompt. RESULT CHECKLIST. Before you use any tool result, check it against this list: 1. Presence and type: every field you need is present and has the right type. 2. Agreement with your request: values that repeat your request (IDs, names, dates, codes) match what you asked for. 3. Plausibility: numbers and categories are sensible (for example, no negative prices or impossible values). 4. Consistency: the result does not contradict itself and is about what you asked. If any check fails, treat the result as incorrect: retry the tool, use another tool that can do the same step, or stop and report which step failed.

sections.title: C Baselines and Published Methods
sections.content: All methods run in the same harness, with the same models, tasks, decoding settings and turn limits. Each prompt follows the design of the cited paper and is adapted to our tasks. We say below which text is the authors own. Checklist (Sun et al., 2024). This arm adds the result checklist above to the system prompt. The source uses task-specific checklists, and ours is general one in the same style. Reviewer (Ta et al., 2026). Before each tool call runs, the agents own model reviews it, and the agent may revise the call (up to five review loops, as in the source). The source uses separate reviewer model and its own prompts. We wrote the prompt below for our tasks, following their design. You are reviewer agent. primary assistant is carrying out users task with tools. Before its provisional tool call is executed, decide whether the call is correct. Check the call against the user request, the tool documentation, and the whole conversation so far, including earlier tool results. Look for: wrong tool, wrong or made-up arguments, arguments copied from tool result that is wrong or inconsistent, skipped or repeated steps, and continuing when the workflow should stop. [...] Reply with JSON only. Outcome Monitors (Panthi and Abdelfattah, 2026). Contracts are mined as above. response that breaks one gets the authors non-binding advisory below, with the retail database replaced by this API. [OUTCOME CONTRACT ADVISORY] The observed result [...] is inconsistent with known invariant of this API. Violation: [...]. This advisory is nonbinding. Treat the result as unreliable and verify or recover using the available documented tools and task context before relying on it. On AgentOrchBench, contracts are mined from clean responses of other tasks, 5-fold by task. LLM judge. This is our own baseline, an LLM judge in the sense of Zheng et al. (2023). After each filter query, fixed judge model (gpt-oss-120b, the same for every agent) sees the task, the request filters, the response and the results of the harnesss own consistency queries, and returns TRUSTWORTHY or SUSPECT with reason, which is appended to the response. We first tried smaller judge (GPT-4o-mini). It called correct responses suspect even when given the passing check numbers, so we used the stronger judge to keep the baseline fair. Controls for evidence, permission and enforcement. LLM judge, no check results uses the same judge and prompt, but the judge sees only the task, the request filters and the response, not the harnesss consistency queries. With + blocking, result the judge calls SUSPECT (or that breaks an Outcome Monitors contract) is withheld, and the final count must come from result the detector accepted, with the same two-rejection answer rule as SilentGuard. Warning + may abstain combines the warning of the full count check (the check SilentGuard uses, which names the failed condition and shows no numbers) with the caution prompt below, which allows the answer that the count cannot be determined. An earlier version used the last-condition check and warning that shows the checks numbers. It gave 63.1% wrong for the warning alone and 12.1% with permission, but misses filter ignored at another position. These ran on 7 models with 2 seeds (Nemotron-3-Ultra on Genentechs internal platform with the same code and grader, counts only). Caution prompt. This text is added to the system prompt. IMPORTANT: tool and API outputs are not always reliable. An API can return HTTP 200 with wrong data, for example by silently ignoring part of your request. Do not blindly trust response. Before answering, check that each response is consistent with what you asked for; if you cannot confirm it, say the count cannot be determined instead of reporting number. Self-verification. The model is told the same every-position check the harness runs and must run it itself before reporting count, or answer that the count cannot be determined. This shows the effect of who runs the check, the model or the harness. Re-query and blind retry. Re-query sends the same query second time and shows both counts. Blind retry sends every request twice and shows only the second response. On ToolMaze it is added to the checklist with Outcome Monitors, so it differs from that arm only by the retry. Harness actions (ablations). These differ in the action after failed count check. Warning appends the check result, and warning + tip also names the recovery tools. The answer gate rejects an answer that repeats flagged count twice and then answers unknown. Enforce accepts only checked counts. Auto-repair recomputes the count through separate 16 routes and shows it only if route passed its own check. Three earlier arms, warning (last condition), its variant with may abstain and the answer gate, check the last condition only. All others use the full check. sections.content: This section answers points reader may raise and that the main text covers only briefly. Each fault type is modeled on kind of API bug. Table 7 lists them, and three kinds occur in the real APIs we probed. These are an ignored parameter in 10 of 15, silently capped page and an ignored filter value  (Table 11)  . The other fault types are not measured in real APIs. SilentGuard also has the fewest wrong answers on the retail schema, cuts wrong answers on those real APIs, and is slightly ahead of the published methods on ToolMaze silent faults, benchmark built by others with different tasks and faults. The method is not limited to counts. It uses whatever checks tool allows. These are an exact identity for count queries, record checks for lists (App. G), the APIs own parameter list for documented APIs, and learned contracts for everything else. Table 1 lists exact checks for other common operations. On ToolMaze, whose workflows book, pay, message and look up records, only learned contracts are available, and SilentGuard is slightly ahead of the published methods on silent faults. Answering unknown is not refusing. Under fault that repeats on every call, the API cannot give the correct count, so the real choice is between wrong number and saying so. On the same tasks with no fault, SilentGuard is as accurate as no guard (84.9% against 84.9%). On real APIs, where the agent can rewrite the query, SilentGuard raises correct answers from 3.5% to 69.5%. Repair releases wrong answers as verified. Auto-repair gives more correct answers on the fault types it was built for, but on unseen fault types it released 49 wrong answers marked as verified  (Table 6)  . wrong answer that says it is verified is worse than no answer.
